query: What single primary estimand for the DT→DC→SCC mediation best balances interpretability and credible identification under staggered adoption?

response.query: What single primary estimand for the DT→DC→SCC mediation best balances interpretability and credible identification under staggered adoption?
response.answer: The primary estimand for DT→DC→SCC mediation in staggered adoption is the weighted average of local average treatment effects (LATE). It balances interpretability and credible identification.

results.title: A Generalized Difference-in-Differences Estimator for Randomized Stepped-Wedge and Observational Staggered Adoption Settings
results.content: Across settings, the analysis of the data generated from staggered treatment adoption requires careful consideration of the desired estimand, assumptions about the treatment effect, consideration of heterogeneity across units, time periods, and treatment regimens, and appropriate consideration of variance and correlation. In the observational staggered adoption setting, approaches to address the biases that can arise in two-way fixed-effects models (see, e.g., Goodman-Bacon (2021) and Imai & Kim (2021)) have included adjusting the interpretation based on the identifying assumptions as in Athey & Imbens (2022), specifying “dynamic” (time-varying) treatment effects as in Sun & Abraham (2021), and isolating, excluding, or weighting effect estimators targeting specific group-time effects as in Callaway & Sant’Anna (2021) and de Chaisemartin & D’Haultfœuille (2020). The first group were designed for the staggered adoption setting- (see Arkhangelsky & Imbens (2024) for a summary), the second group specifically target the effect in the first period on treatment, and the last estimator uses only vertical comparisons.

results.title: Two-way fixed effects instrumental variable regressions in staggered DID-IV designs.I am grateful to Daiji Kawaguchi and Ryo Okui for their continued guidance and support. All errors are my own.
results.content: Under staggered DID-IV designs, a causal interpretation of the TWFEIV estimand hinges on the stable effects of the instrument on the treatment and the outcome over time. Because we assume the staggered assignment of the instrument across units, if we focus on the TWFE coefficient on in the first stage or the reduced form regression, we can show that it is equal to a weighted average of all possible DID estimators of the treatment or the outcome from the decomposition result for the TWFE estimator shown by Goodman-Bacon (2021). We first show that in settings with the staggered adoption of the instrument across units, the TWFEIV estimator is equal to a weighted average of all possible Wald-DID estimators arising from the three types of the DID-IV design: Unexposed/Exposed, Exposed/Not Yet Exposed, and Exposed/Exposed Shift designs. Based on the decomposition result, we then show that in staggered DID-IV designs, the TWFEIV estimand is equal to a weighted average of all possible cohort specific local average treatment effect on the treated parameters, but some weights can be negative.

results.title: [2405.12083] Instrumented Difference-in-Differences with Heterogeneous Treatment Effects
results.content: # Title:Instrumented Difference-in-Differences with Heterogeneous Treatment Effects. View a PDF of the paper titled Instrumented Difference-in-Differences with Heterogeneous Treatment Effects, by Sho Miyaji. > Abstract:Many studies exploit variation in policy adoption timing across units as an instrument for treatment. This paper formalizes the underlying identification strategy as an instrumented difference-in-differences (DID-IV). In this design, a Wald-DID estimand, which scales the DID estimand of the outcome by the DID estimand of the treatment, captures the local average treatment effect on the treated (LATET). We extend the canonical DID-IV design to multiple period settings with the staggered adoption of the instrument across units. Moreover, we propose a credible estimation method in this design that is robust to treatment effect heterogeneity. We illustrate the empirical relevance of our findings, estimating returns to schooling in the United Kingdom. In this application, the two-way fixed effects instrumental variable regression, the conventional approach to implement DID-IV designs, yields a negative estimate. **** Mon, 20 May 2024 14:52:39 UTC (4,738 KB). **** Wed, 22 May 2024 00:55:38 UTC (4,738 KB). **** Mon, 22 Jul 2024 15:31:02 UTC (4,738 KB). **** Tue, 23 Jul 2024 02:15:58 UTC (4,738 KB). **[v5]** Tue, 7 Jan 2025 13:36:12 UTC (2,398 KB). ## Access Paper:. results.title: Identification - The Key to Credible Causal Inference | Murat Unal
results.content: # Identification - The Key to Credible Causal Inference. #### Improve your causal IQ and build trust in your causal inference by mastering identification. Behind this process are two distinct concepts: identification and estimation, and only by mastering both can we get better at establishing causality from associations observed in the data. As such, in this article we will discuss in detail why identification has precedence over estimation and why causal inference will fail without it. Similarly, in causal inference, identification allows us to not only set the stage correctly for estimation but also build trust in our work. As such, to be able to conduct an identification analysis and to communicate it clearly is an underappreciated yet powerful skill that we must master if we want to improve our causal IQ as well as build trust in our causal inference. Essentially, identification means laying out the assumptions needed for a statistical estimate we obtain from the data to be given a causal interpretation. It also means making a case for why the assumptions are plausible and therefore the association we find in the data identifies the causal estimand, i.e. the ATE, that we are after and can be trusted as a causal relationship. Simply put, if identification fails, in other words if the assumptions behind our causal inference are not plausible, then no modeling or estimation approach can take us beyond association. So, what are the main identification strategies then for causal inference? Basically, every estimation method that we encounter ranging from a simple difference in means to the latest causal machine learning relies on one of these identification strategies [2]. Hence, for practitioners who want to get better at causal inference, it makes more sense to first understand this strategy and its assumptions in detail before moving into studying the various estimation methods. Let’s conclude this piece by reiterating that causal inference starts with identification and the most credible causal inferences are those that have a clear and convincing identification strategy, not those that have the most sophisticated estimation methods. Data science practitioners who want their causal inferences to be taken seriously, need to master identification.

results.title: Staggered DiD versus traditional DiD - What is different? | Welcome to my homepage!
results.content: One of these papers is the paper by Athey and Imbens (2018) which concludes that under random treatment assignment the standard Difference-In-Differences estimator is an unbiased estimator of a particular weighted average causal effect. To derive their results, Athey and Imbens (2018) consider a setting with i=1,…,N individuals and t=1,…,T time periods, with a binary treatment being first adopted in t=T+1. They then define a fraction of individuals belonging to each timing-treatment-group, and the population average of the potential outcome in period t for adoption date a:. Put differently, there is no causal effect of an early or late adoption of the treatment on the outcome of interest. They interprete the DiD estimand under the random adoption assumption, therefore leading to a different result than previous paper analyzing the estimate. They then show that the staggered DiD estimator is a weighted average of simple estimators for the causal effect of changes in the adoption dates, which they call \(\tau\_{t, aa'}\).
